text:
🇲🇽📈 <u>TAMAULIPAS GROWS 5.2%, LANDS $20.7 BILLION INVESTMENT PIPELINE</u>

Tamaulipas grew 5.2% in the first quarter of 2026 — the state contributing most to national growth while Mexico’s economy overall advanced just 0.3%, per INEGI data reported by El Economista. The state has 171 confirmed investment projects worth 20,675 million dollars, says state economy secretary Ninfa Cantú Deándar.

Nearshoring in Mexico’s northeast isn’t a slogan. It’s a pipeline.

🇲🇽💼 <u>CDMX LEADS MEXICO WITH RECORD 3.67 MILLION FORMAL JOBS</u>

Mexico City kept the top national spot in formal employment at the close of July: 3,677,103 workers registered with IMSS — and 84.17% of them hold permanent positions. The post-World Cup adjustment never became a jobs collapse: losses in services were absorbed by industry and transport, which added 35,319 new registrations in July alone.

The capital’s average daily base salary reached 800.44 pesos, up 13.94% in a year. Formal work, rising pay.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>MEXICO EXPOSES 560,000-ACCOUNT BOT NETWORK AGAINST SHEINBAUM</u>

That flood of simultaneous anti-Sheinbaum posts on social media isn’t a multitude of outraged citizens — it’s a structure built to look like one. Mexico’s Presidential Legal Counsel says a digital amplification network against the President and the Fourth Transformation links media outlets, commentators, political figures and over 560,000 attack accounts, bots and trolls.

“This network is not organic,” said counsel Luisa María Alcalde. Manufactured outrage, at industrial scale.

🇲🇽🚛 <u>CARGO THEFT ON MEXICAN HIGHWAYS DOWN 19%</u>

Robberies of cargo trucks on Mexico’s federal highways fell 19.41% in the first half of 2026 — 607 fewer cases than the same period last year, National Guard commander Guillermo Briseño Lobera reported, citing SESNSP victim-report data. June alone was down 11.2% year-on-year, and highway vigilance will be reinforced further.

The quiet numbers the “failed state” headlines never mention.

🇲🇽💧 <u>CONAGUA SHUTS SIX ILLEGAL WELLS IN SAN LUIS POTOSÍ</u>

Mexico’s water authority Conagua clausurated six irregular extraction points in the Vanegas-Catorce aquifer, in the Altiplano of San Luis Potosí, acting on complaints from residents of Estación Catorce. Inspectors found wells with no meters — meaning nobody knew how much water was being pumped — and inconsistencies in concession titles.

The operation ran with the Agrarian Prosecutor’s office, the INAH and the ejido commissariat at the table. Inspections continue across the region. Water is a national patrimony again, not a free-for-all.

🇲🇽🇨🇺 <u>MEXICO COLLECTS 4 TONS OF MEDICAL AID FOR CUBA ON FIDEL CENTENNIAL</u>

While Washington tightens the blockade, Mexico City’s Zócalo is filling up with medicine, medical supplies and powdered milk for Cuba. The Va por Cuba collective’s four-day drive — its fourth — aims to beat the 4 tons sent in previous editions, and this time it answers President Sheinbaum’s own call to solidarity. “The ties of friendship, solidarity and support with Cuba are ancestral,” organizer Francisco Rosas told La Jornada.

A century after Fidel’s birth: the empire blockades, Mexico sends medicine.

🇲🇽📈 <u>SINALOA INDUSTRY GROWS 10.4% — FOUR TIMES THE NATIONAL RATE</u>

Sinaloa posted one of Mexico's strongest industrial performances in April 2026: 10.4% annual growth against a 2.4% national average, according to INEGI's IMAIEF — sixth place nationwide, tied with Yucatán. Construction led with a 24.9% jump, more than double the national 10.5%.

Hidalgo (21.0%), Nayarit (16.2%), Oaxaca (13.1%), Guerrero (11.9%) and Veracruz (11.2%) topped the table — the industrial map is shifting south and toward 4T-governed states.

🇲🇽🥊 <u>PILARES: WHERE CDMX YOUTH TURN WORKSHOPS INTO CAREERS</u>

The 122nd edition of Dialogos PILARES put faces on Mexico City's community-education model. Boxer Miranda González won medals at the indigenous olympiad two years running after training at PILARES: "PILARES has helped me feel that confidence." Leibniz Ramírez trained in image design and now works as a professional colorist. Fernanda Mercado went from free dance workshops to the Ollin Yolliztli Cultural Center.

Free public training, real careers. That's what a city that invests in its youth looks like.
